title: Bursty Stream Smoothing & Tool Saga — PRD Draft
content:
Overview:
This doc sketches a focused PRD for handling bursty inbound traffic for the Hosted streaming API while improving the ergonomics of tool-calling and structured partial outputs in client SDKs. Goal is pragmatic: reduce tail latency/regret during traffic microbursts, keep developer-facing surface minimal, and ensure transparent telemetry for cost/quality tradeoffs.

Context / Problem:
- Customers using streaming chat + tool calls see latency spikes when frontend traffic arrives in short bursts (e.g., many short conversations starting simultaneously).
- Existing runtime batches aggressively which helps cost, but bursty arrivals either: (a) wait for batch windows -> increased first-token latency, or (b) start many under-filled workers -> cost blowups and cold-start issues.
- Tool calls complicate streaming: tool responses may be delayed, partial, or produce structured payloads that need incremental delivery. SDKs today either buffer everything or implement fragile hacks.

Primary goals:
1) Improve p50/p95 first-token latency under bursty load without regressing p99 for steady-state.
2) Provide clear, low-friction tool-call handshake semantics that work over streaming partial outputs.
3) Provide an SDK-friendly compact frame model for incremental structured JSON and resumable sessions.
4) Expose telemetry and toggles so customers can trade cost vs latency (auto-smooth heuristics with opt-out).

Non-goals:
- Re-architecting the serving runtime in full; prefer runtime knobs + lightweight routing changes.
- Removing support for large, batch-optimized offline workloads.

Proposed approach (high level):
A) Microburst-aware admission + fast-path workers
  - Introduce a fast-path ephemeral worker pool optimized for short requests (<= 256 tokens expected).
  - Admission logic: detect session arrival rate spike at per-customer+region level; allocate fast-path capacity if short requests dominate for a sliding window (10s).
  - Fast-path uses lower batching thresholds (time-window 3–10ms) and constrained KV cache warmups.
  - Fallback: if request exceeds expected size or exceeds token budget, seamlessly route to standard pool mid-stream (with token continuity via session id + transparent rekeying).

B) Smoothing layer (queue + hedging):
  - Local smoothing queue in front of runtime that can: (1) coalesce short-sessions for a micro-batch, (2) hedge small batches with one speculative fast worker when latency budget is tight.
  - Hedging policy: for requests with latency SLO < 200ms, after 15ms of waiting, start a speculative fast-path call to reduce tail. First completed response wins; runtime tracks double-run cost.
  - Configurable per-customer: enable/disable hedging, hedging aggressiveness (sensitivity). Default off for free tier.

C) Tool-call handshake & partial structured output model:
  - Streaming frame model extended with three frame classes: TEXT_DELTA, TOOL_CALL, TOOL_RESULT_PART, TOOL_RESULT_FINAL, META.
  - TOOL_CALL frame contains: tool_id, call_id, optional args-preview (truncated), and a call-routing hint. (We keep frame small and typed.)
  - TOOL_RESULT_PART frames stream partial tool output (useful for long-running tools). Each part includes sequence index and content part. TOOL_RESULT_FINAL signals completion and canonical JSON payload (if available) or a pointer to storage.
  - If tool result is not yet available within client-visible window, SDK surfaces a \"pending tool\" sentinel in the stream and then patches with TOOL_RESULT_PART/FINAL frames when they arrive.
  - Safety: tool outputs must be validated server-side before FINAL frame emission; partial frames are clearly marked as untrusted until FINAL arrives.

D) Compact frame encoding (SDK ergonomics):
  - Use a minimal wire format over streaming (newline-delimited JSON frames; each frame is small JSON with type/fields). This avoids complex websocket subprotocols and integrates easily with HTTP/2 or SSE.
  - SDK helpers: provide incremental parser that emits events: onTextDelta, onToolCall, onToolResultPart, onToolResultFinal, onMeta. SDK will expose a single-stream generator/async iterator with a small dialect for resumption.
  - Resume semantics: stream snapshots every N seconds (configurable). If client disconnects, they can reconnect with resume_token and receive missing frames (idempotent replay).
  - Backpressure: SDK exposes an optional token-based backpressure hint: clients may signal tail-drop or slow-consume. Runtime will reduce speculative hedging and prefer batching when backpressure indicated.

E) Developer UX patterns (examples):
  - Simple use-case (chat + tool): SDK incremental generator yields text deltas; client renders progressively. When a TOOL_CALL frame arrives, SDK pauses tool-local UI button until TOOL_RESULT_PART/FINAL patched; developer can show spinner + partial progress percent if available.
  - Offline / mobile: SDK can choose to buffer until first TOOL_RESULT_PART if app is backgrounded. Resume token ensures session continues.

Acceptance criteria / success metrics:
- Latency: p50 first-token for short-chat workload improves by >= 25% during simulated burst tests (JIRA STREAM-678 load profile).
- Cost: hedging increases cost per-request by < 8% on average for enabled customers (monitor per-customer cost delta).
- Tool UX: 95% of tool calls that return within 2s should deliver at least one TOOL_RESULT_PART within 500ms of tool-response-start.
- Resume: reconnect+resume should restore missing frames in 99.9% of simulated disconnects in 10k test runs.
- SDK adoption: new Node/Python streaming SDKs with compact-frame parser released; internal dogfood by 3 teams within 4 weeks.

Telemetry & observability (minimum):
- per-request: admission path (fast/standard), hedged? (true/false), batch_size_on_dispatch, first_token_latency_ms, total_tokens, tool_calls_count, tool_call_latency_ms, resume_attempts
- per-customer dashboards: cost delta attributable to hedging/smoothing, p50/p95 first-token over time, tool-call success rate & time-to-first-part
- distributed traces: mark speculative duplications so we can attribute double-execution cost.

Open design tradeoffs / questions:
- Fast-path correctness: migrating a request mid-stream (fast->standard) requires robust KV cache continuity. Do we accept small coherence gaps for performance? (engineering to evaluate; see API-3245).
- Hedging threshold tuning: default values need production calibration to avoid cost surprises. Ops toggle must be immediate and observable.
- Partial tool trust model: do we allow client-side speculative UX actions on PART frames? Likely no for high-risk tools; provide opt-in flag per-tool.
- Frame format: we propose newline-JSON for compatibility, but binary compact formats (CBOR/msgpack) yield wire savings. Should we offer opt-in binary?

Rollout plan (phases):
1) Internal prototype + e2e simulation (4 weeks): implement admission + fast-path stub in serving runtime, simulate microburst by replaying production traces.
2) SDK alpha + dogfood (3 weeks): ship Node/Python adapter with parser and resume tests to internal teams (search infra, chat product).
3) Canary on hosted infra (2 weeks): enable for 1% of traffic with telemetry and automatic rollback.
4) Gradual ramp (to 25% -> 100%) with ops toggles for hedging.

Operational playbook / guardrails:
- Auto-disable hedging if per-customer cost spike above threshold within 15 minutes.
- Emergency toggle in console to force all requests to standard pool.
- Alerting: increase in speculative duplication cost > 10% over baseline, p99 first-token regression > 50ms.

Implementation notes for eng teams:
- Serving runtime: add lightweight admission probe that observes recent short-session ratio per-customer. Prefer in-memory rate windows instead of external calls.
- Router: must support mid-stream routing metadata to allow resume on handoff.
- SDK: supply convenience types and examples for React/Vue streaming UIs; mobile examples for iOS/Android should show background-friendly resume.

Docs & developer-facing collateral needed:
- Quickstart: "Progressive streams + tools in 10 minutes" (sample app: fine-grained tool calls with partial output)
- FAQ: hedging cost model, when to disable, how to opt-in binary frames
- Migration guide: existing non-streaming tool-call users who want to switch to progressive frames.

Open TODOs (short list):
- [ ] Design binary frame proposal and cost/latency comparison (engineering)
- [ ] Run hedging cost sensitivity matrix on 10 customers (platform)
- [ ] Draft SDK API for resume_token and backpressure hints (DX)
- [ ] Security sign-off for partial tool outputs and server-side validation (security)

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally pragmatic; prefer incremental runtime changes + richer client SDK primitives rather than an ambitious protocol overhaul.
- Looking for feedback on: hedging defaults, tool-part trust model, and mid-stream routing complexity.

References:
- JIRA: API-3245 (fast-path admission design)
- JIRA: STREAM-678 (bursty-load simulation)
- GH: https://github.com/redwood-inference/hosted-api/pull/789 (initial frame parser prototype)
